question.problem: At which points on the curve $3y{x}^{2}=48+3x{y}^{2}$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i-j?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y{x}^{2} & =48+3x{y}^{2} \\ 3y{x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2} & =48\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=3y{x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=48.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3y{x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(3y{x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2})j \\  & =(3{x}^{2}-6xy)i-(6xy-3{y}^{2})j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot (i-j)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot (i-j) & =0 \\ ((3{x}^{2}-6xy)i-(6xy-3{y}^{2})j)\cdot (i-j) & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-6xy+6xy-3{y}^{2} & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-y)(x+y) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=y$ or $x=-y.$ Substituting $x=y$ into the equation of our curve gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y{x}^{2} & =48+3x{y}^{2} \\ 3y{y}^{2} & =48+3y{y}^{2} \\ 3{y}^{3} & =48+3{y}^{3} \\ 0 & =48\end{aligned}
$$

Since we get a false statement, we conclude that does not exist points of the form $(x,x)$ on the curve. Substituting $x=-y$ into the equation of our curve gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y{x}^{2} & =48+3x{y}^{2} \\ 3y(-y)^{2} & =48+3(-y){y}^{2} \\ 3{y}^{3} & =48-3{y}^{3} \\ 6{y}^{3} & =48 \\ {y}^{3} & =8 \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{8} \\ y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $y=2$, we get $x=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,2).$
